title: De Senectute
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

passages.original: LAELIUS. Est, ut dicis, Cato; sed fortasse dixerit quispiam tibi propter opes et copias et dignitatem tuam tolerabiliorem senectutem videri, id autem non posse multis contingere.
passages.english: LAELIUS. It is as you say, Cato; but perhaps someone might say that old age seems more bearable to you because of your wealth and resources and your standing, but that this cannot fall to the lot of many.

passages.original: quaestor deinde quadriennio post factus sum, quem magistratum gessi consulibus Tuditano et Cethego, cum quidem ille admodum senex suasor legis Cinciae de donis et muneribus fuit. hic et bella gerebat ut adulescens, cum plane grandis esset, et Hannibalem iuveniliter exsultantem patientia sua molliebat; de quo praeclare familiaris noster Ennius: unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem;noenum rumores ponebat ante salutem;ergo plusque magisque viri nunc gloria claret.
passages.english: Then four years later I was made quaestor, an office I held when Tuditanus and Cethegus were consuls, at the time when he, now a very old man, spoke in favour of the Cincian law on gifts and fees. He both waged wars like a young man, though he was plainly advanced in years, and by his patience wore down Hannibal as he exulted with youthful spirit; of him our friend Ennius said finely: "One man by delaying restored the state for us; he did not put rumours before safety; so now the glory of the man shines more and more."
passages.notes: The subject "he" is Quintus Fabius Maximus (Cunctator), the recapturer of Tarentum mentioned in the preceding context. The Ennius verses are run together in the source with semicolons; rendered here as continuous quotation.

passages.original: nec tamen omnes possunt esse Scipiones aut Maximi, ut urbium expugnationes, ut pedestris navalisve pugnas, ut bella a se gesta, ut triumphos recordentur. est etiam quiete et pure atque eleganter actae aetatis placida ac lenis senectus, qualem accepimus Platonis, qui uno et octogesimo anno scribens est mortuus, qualem Isocratis, qui eum librum, qui Panathenaicus inscribitur, quarto nonagesimo anno scripsisse dicit vixitque quinquennium postea; cuius magister Leontinus Gorgias centum et septem complevit annos, neque umquam in suo studio atque opere cessavit.
passages.english: Yet not everyone can be a Scipio or a Maximus, so as to recall the storming of cities, battles on land or sea, wars waged by themselves, and triumphs. There is also the calm and gentle old age of a life spent quietly, purely and with refinement, such as we are told Plato's was, who died at his writing in his eighty-first year; such as that of Isocrates, who says that he wrote the book entitled the Panathenaicus in his ninety-fourth year, and he lived five years after that; his teacher Gorgias of Leontini completed one hundred and seven years, and never once ceased from his study and his work.

passages.original: sua enim vitia insipientes et suam culpam in senectutem conferunt, quod non faciebat is, cuius modo mentionem feci, Ennius: sic ut fortis equus, spatio qui saepe supremo vicit Olympia, nunc senio confectus quiescit.equi fortis et victoris senectuti comparat suam; quem quidem probe meminisse potestis; anno enim undevicesimo post eius mortem hi consules, T.
passages.english: For foolish people blame old age for their own faults and their own failings, which that man I mentioned just now, Ennius, did not do: "Just as a brave horse, which often won at Olympia on the final lap, now rests, worn out with old age." He compares his own old age to that of a brave and victorious horse; and you can surely remember him well, for in the nineteenth year after his death the present consuls, T.
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at "T."; it continues in the following passage ("Flamininus and M'. Acilius were made [consuls]").

passages.original: tamen is, cum sententia senatus inclinaret ad pacem cum Pyrrho foedusque faciendum, non dubitavit dicere illa, quae versibus persecutus est Ennius: quo vobis mentes, rectae quae stare solebant antehac, dementis sese flexere viai? ceteraque gravissime, notum enim vobis carmen est, et tamen ipsius Appi exstat oratio. atque haec ille egit septemdecim annis post alterum consulatum, cum inter duos consulatus anni decem interfuissent censorque ante superiorem consulatum fuisset, ex quo intellegitur Pyrrhi bello grandem sane fuisse, et tamen sic a patribus accepimus.
passages.english: Yet he, when the opinion of the senate was inclining toward making peace and a treaty with Pyrrhus, did not hesitate to say those things which Ennius set out in verse: "Where have your minds, which used to stand upright before, turned themselves, off the road into madness?" and the rest, most weightily; for the poem is known to you, and besides, Appius' own speech survives. And he did this seventeen years after his second consulship, though ten years had passed between his two consulships and he had been censor before his earlier consulship; from which it is understood that he was certainly a very old man at the time of the war with Pyrrhus, and yet that is what we have received from our fathers.
passages.notes: "He" is Appius Claudius Caecus, named later in the passage. "dementis ... viai" (archaic genitive) is taken as "of the mad road".

passages.original: quamquam in aliis minus hoc mirum est, nemo enim est tam senex qui se annum non putet posse vivere; sed idem in eis elaborant, quae sciunt nihil ad se omnino pertinere: serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint, ut ait Statius noster in Synephebis.
passages.english: And yet in other matters this is less surprising, for no one is so old that he does not think he can live a year; but these same men labour at things which they know do not concern them at all: "he plants trees to benefit another generation," as our Statius says in the Synephebi.
passages.notes: Statius is Caecilius Statius, the comic poet; Synephebi ("The Young Comrades") is his play.

passages.original: sed videtis, ut senectus non modo languida atque iners non sit, verum etiam sit operosa et semper agens aliquid et moliens, tale scilicet, quale cuiusque studium in superiore vita fuit. quid, qui etiam addiscunt aliquid, ut et Solonem versibus gloriantem videmus, qui se cotidie aliquid addiscentem dicit senem fieri. et ego feci, qui litteras Graecas senex didici, quas quidem sic avide arripui quasi diuturnam sitim explere cupiens, ut ea ipsa mihi nota essent, quibus me nunc exemplis uti videtis.
passages.english: But you see how old age is not only not feeble and sluggish, but is even busy and always doing and undertaking something, such, of course, as each person's pursuit was in his earlier life. What of those who even learn something more, as we see Solon boasting in verse, who says that he grows old learning something more every day? And I have done so, who learned Greek literature as an old man; I seized on it so eagerly, as if longing to quench a long thirst, that those very things became known to me which you now see me using as examples.

passages.original: Cyrus quidem apud Xenophontem eo sermone, quem moriens habuit, cum admodum senex esset, negat se umquam sensisse senectutem suam imbecilliorem factam quam adulescentia fuisset. ego L. Metellum memini puer, qui, cum quadriennio post alterum consulatum pontifex maximus factus esset, viginti et duos annos ei sacerdotio praefuit, ita bonis esse viribus extremo tempore aetatis, ut adulescentiam non requireret.
passages.english: Cyrus, indeed, in Xenophon, in the discourse which he gave when dying, when he was a very old man, denies that he ever felt his old age to have become weaker than his youth had been. I remember as a boy Lucius Metellus, who, having been made pontifex maximus four years after his second consulship, presided over that priesthood for twenty-two years, being in such good strength at the very end of his life that he did not miss his youth.

passages.original: videtisne, ut apud Homerum saepissime Nestor de virtutibus suis praedicet? Tertiam enim aetatem hominum videbat, nec erat ei verendum ne vera praedicans de se nimis videretur aut insolens aut loquax. etenim, ut ait Homerus, ex eius lingua melle dulcior fluebat oratio;
passages.english: Do you see how very often in Homer Nestor proclaims his own virtues? For he was seeing the third generation of men, and he had no need to fear that, in proclaiming true things about himself, he would seem either too arrogant or too talkative. For, as Homer says, speech sweeter than honey flowed from his tongue;

passages.original: caret epulis exstructisque mensis et frequentibus poculis. caret ergo etiam vinulentia et cruditate et insomniis. sed si aliquid dandum est voluptati, quoniam eius blanditiis non facile obsistimus, divine enim Plato escam malorum appellat voluptatem quod ea videlicet homines capiantur ut pisces, quamquam immoderatis epulis caret senectus, modicis tamen conviviis delectari potest. C. Duellium M. F., qui Poenos classe primus devicerat, redeuntem a cena senem saepe videbam puer;
passages.english: [Old age] lacks banquets, heaped-up tables and frequent cups. It therefore also lacks drunkenness, indigestion and sleeplessness. But if something must be granted to pleasure, since we do not easily resist its allurements (for Plato divinely calls pleasure the bait of evils, because, evidently, men are caught by it like fish), although old age lacks immoderate banquets, it can nevertheless take delight in moderate dinner parties. As a boy I often saw Gaius Duellius, son of Marcus, who had been the first to defeat the Carthaginians with a fleet, returning from dinner as an old man;
passages.notes: "insomniis" could also mean "bad dreams"; "sleeplessness" is taken here.

passages.original: Licini Crassi et pontifici et civilis iuris studio loquar aut de huius P. Scipionis, qui his paucis diebus pontifex maximus factus est? atque eos omnis, quos commemoravi, his studiis flagrantis senes vidimus. M. vero Cethegum, quem recte suadae medullam dixit Ennius, quanto studio exerceri in dicendo videbamus etiam senem! quae sunt igitur epularum aut ludorum aut scortorum voluptates cum his voluptatibus comparandae? atque haec quidem studia doctrinae, quae quidem prudentibus et bene institutis pariter cum aetate crescunt, ut honestum illud Solonis sit, quod ait versiculo quodam, ut ante dixi, senescere se multa in dies addiscentem, qua voluptate animi nulla certe potest esse maior.
passages.english: Shall I speak of Licinius Crassus' pursuit of both pontifical and civil law, or of that of this Publius Scipio, who within these last few days was made pontifex maximus? And all those whom I have mentioned we have seen as old men burning with these pursuits. And Marcus Cethegus, whom Ennius rightly called "the marrow of persuasion", with what zeal we saw him exercising himself in speaking even as an old man! What pleasures, then, of banquets or games or harlots are to be compared with these pleasures? And these are the pursuits of learning, which for the wise and well-trained grow along with their age, so that there is honour in that saying of Solon, which he speaks in a certain little verse, as I said before, that he grows old learning many things more each day; and than this pleasure of the mind there certainly can be none greater.
passages.notes: The opening question begins in the context ("What of P."), so the first name is the continuation of "P. Licinius Crassus". The last sentence's syntax is loose in the Latin ("atque haec quidem studia doctrinae" lacks a main verb); rendered with "are" supplied.

passages.original: quam copiose ab eo agri cultura laudatur in eo libro, qui est de tuenda re familiari, qui Oeconomicus inscribitur! atque ut intellegatis nihil ei tam regale videri quam studium agri colendi, Socrates in eo libro loquitur cum Critobulo Cyrum minorem, Persarum regem, praestantem ingenio atque imperi gloria, cum Lysander Lacedaemonius, vir summae virtutis, venisset ad eum Sardis eique dona a sociis attulisset, et ceteris in rebus communem erga Lysandrum atque humanum fuisse et ei quendam consaeptum agrum diligenter consitum ostendisse.
passages.english: How fully is agriculture praised by him in that book which is about managing one's household property, which is entitled the Oeconomicus! And so that you may understand that nothing seemed to him so kingly as the pursuit of farming, Socrates in that book, speaking with Critobulus, says that Cyrus the Younger, king of the Persians, outstanding in talent and in the glory of his rule, when Lysander the Spartan, a man of the highest virtue, had come to him at Sardis and brought him gifts from the allies, was both courteous and kind toward Lysander in other matters and showed him a certain enclosed field carefully planted.
passages.notes: "Him" is Xenophon (from context). Cicero calls Cyrus the Younger "king", though he was not in fact king.

passages.original: vetatque Pythagoras iniussu imperatoris, id est dei, de praesidio et statione vitae decedere. Solonis quidem sapientis est elogium, quo se negat velle suam mortem dolore amicorum et lamentis vacare. volt, credo, se esse carum suis. sed haud scio an melius Ennius: nemo me lacrumis decoret, neque funera fletu faxit.non censet lugendam esse mortem, quam immortalitas consequatur.
passages.english: And Pythagoras forbids [us] to depart from the guard-post and station of life without the command of our commander, that is, of god. There is indeed an epitaph of the wise Solon in which he says he does not want his death to be without the grief and laments of his friends. He wants, I suppose, to be dear to his own people. But I rather think Ennius [puts it] better: "Let no one honour me with tears, nor make my funeral with weeping." He thinks that death should not be mourned, since immortality follows it.
passages.notes: "elogium" here means a short verse inscription or saying, rendered "epitaph".

passages.original: apud Xenophontem autem moriens Cyrus maior haec dicit: “nolite arbitrari, o mihi carissimi filii, me, cum a vobis discessero, nusquam aut nullum fore. nec enim, dum eram vobiscum, animum meum videbatis, sed eum esse in hoc corpore ex eis rebus quas gerebam intellegebatis.
passages.english: In Xenophon, moreover, the elder Cyrus, when dying, says this: "Do not think, my dearest sons, that when I have departed from you I shall be nowhere or nothing. For even while I was with you, you did not see my soul, but you understood that it was in this body from the things that I was doing.
